analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent and eliminates taxes on stock dividends, capital gains, and inherited estates.
analysis.headline: The bill got zero cosponsors and no committee action in the Senate Finance Committee, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the 2001 tax-cut law (EGTRRA) permanent by repealing its expiration date, and moved up every major tax cut in it. It would have cut the top tax rates faster, ended the estate tax in 2005 instead of 2010, cut the capital gains tax rate to 10%, and eliminated federal income tax on stock dividends entirely. It also raised retirement account contribution limits and pushed the age for mandatory retirement withdrawals from 70½ to 75.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and investors gain the most: a 10% capital gains rate and a full exclusion of dividends from domestic public companies would largely eliminate tax on investment income from stocks [S2][S3]. The wealthiest households gain again from ending the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes in 2005, a tax that by design falls only on the largest inheritances [S2][S3]. Workers with 401(k)s, 457 plans, or IRAs gain by being able to shelter more money sooner ($15,000 for 401(k)-type plans, $5,000 for IRAs) and delay mandatory withdrawals to 75 [S3]. Anyone with investment losses gains from raising the deductible capital loss limit from $3,000 to $10,000, indexed to inflation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, making its tax cuts permanent rather than expiring [S2][S3].
Accelerates the individual income tax rate reductions so the lower rates arrive years earlier [S2][S3].
Ends the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax as of 2005 instead of 2010 [S2][S3].
Caps the capital gains tax rate at 10% for individuals, including for alternative minimum tax purposes [S3].
Excludes 100% of dividends from domestic, publicly traded C corporations from taxable income [S2][S3].
Raises 401(k) and 457 plan contribution limits to $15,000 and IRA deductible contributions to $5,000, effective in 2003 [S3].
Raises the mandatory retirement plan distribution age from 70½ to 75 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, in the form of foregone revenue, which ultimately means borrowing or future taxes. Because capital gains, dividends, and taxable estates are heavily concentrated among higher-income households, the largest tax savings flow to them, while the lost revenue and any resulting deficits or spending pressure are shared by everyone [S2][S3]. The bill's non-binding 'sense of the Senate' also points toward tort reform and deregulation, which would narrow ordinary people's ability to sue over injuries [S3].

drawbacks.text: Eliminating dividend and capital gains taxes and accelerating estate tax repeal would sharply reduce federal revenue, with the largest benefits going to households with the most invested wealth [S2][S3].
Ending the estate tax in 2005 removes a tax that applied only to the largest estates, concentrating its benefit among the wealthiest families [S2][S3].
The bill includes only a non-binding statement that Congress should safeguard pensions and enact tort reform and deregulation — none of which would actually happen by passing this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions genuinely help middle-class savers: higher 401(k) and IRA limits, a higher capital-loss deduction, and later mandatory withdrawals. But the bill's dominant effect — full dividend exclusion, a 10% capital gains rate, and early estate tax repeal — is a large, permanent tax reduction aimed at investment income and large inheritances, which are concentrated at the top. The revenue cost is broad-based, so the bill on net shifts the tax burden toward work and wages and away from wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the 'Contract With Investors' on January 7, 2003 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Kyl delivered introductory remarks on January 13, 2003; that was the last recorded action [S5].
The Finance Committee never took the bill up, and no vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one acted on it, so the status quo held: investors and large estates did not get the accelerated tax cuts, and the Treasury kept the revenue. Supporters of the bill's ideas pursued them elsewhere in 2003 rather than through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; the bill's supporters gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 7, 2003 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no party split is visible in the record; the bill itself was a Republican-sponsored tax cut.

industries.note: The bill caps the capital gains rate at 10% and fully excludes stock dividends from income tax, removing most tax on equity investment returns. Those savings accrue overwhelmingly to households that own stock, while the lost revenue is shared by all taxpayers.

Accelerating estate and generation-skipping tax repeal to 2005 lets the largest inheritances pass untaxed years early. The estate tax by design touches only estates above multi-million-dollar thresholds.

Tax-free dividends and a 10% capital gains rate increase the after-tax return on stocks and funds, supporting demand for brokerage, mutual fund, and retirement plan products. Higher IRA and 401(k) limits also channel more money through these institutions.
